title: The King of the Jews Crucified
summary: At dawn the council hands Jesus over to Pontius Pilate, who, pressed by the chief priests and the crowd, releases the rebel Barabbas and sentences Jesus to be crucified. Soldiers mock him as king, Simon of Cyrene carries his cross, and he is crucified at Golgotha between two robbers under a charge that reads THE KING OF THE JEWS. After three hours of darkness he cries out in the words of Psalm 22 and dies; the temple curtain is torn, a Roman centurion confesses him as the Son of God, and Joseph of Arimathea buries him in a rock tomb while women watch.
story: This is the climax of Mark's Gospel. The book's first line called Jesus the Son of God, and throughout the story demons have known it while human beings struggled to see it. Now, at the moment of his death, a Gentile soldier says it. Every prediction of the passion has been fulfilled: Jesus has been handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, spat on, flogged, and killed. His disciples have fled, and only women watch from a distance. The chapter shows the kingship of Jesus in the most unlikely form, enthroned on a cross with a criminal on his right and on his left, the places James and John had asked for in 10:37. His burial prepares for the final chapter: his death is certain, the tomb is known, and witnesses saw where he was laid.
historical:
Pontius Pilate governed Judea as prefect from about AD 26 to 36. An inscription discovered at Caesarea Maritima in 1961 bears his name and title, and Josephus and the Jewish philosopher Philo describe him as harsh and provocative toward Jewish sensibilities. The Sanhedrin could not carry out an execution on its own authority, so it brought Jesus to Pilate on a charge that Rome would care about: claiming to be King of the Jews, which implied rebellion against Caesar. Barabbas was a rebel held for murder during an uprising, one of many disturbances in the period. The custom of releasing a prisoner at the feast is attested only in the Gospels, but governors did grant amnesties, and the practice is plausible.

Crucifixion was the Roman punishment for slaves, violent criminals, and rebels, designed to be slow, public, and humiliating. Victims were flogged, forced to carry the crossbeam, and nailed or tied to the cross, often dying over hours or days of exhaustion and suffocation. In 1968 an ossuary (a bone box) found in Jerusalem held the heel bone of a crucified man with a nail still through it, confirming that victims were sometimes nailed. The charge was often written on a placard. Jewish law required that a hanged body not remain overnight (Deuteronomy 21:22-23), which is why Joseph acted before the Sabbath began at sundown.
cultural:
The soldiers' mockery parodies a royal investiture: purple was the color of kings and emperors, the thorny crown imitates a victor's wreath, and Hail, King of the Jews mimics the salute Hail, Caesar. The Praetorium was the governor's headquarters in Jerusalem, probably Herod's former palace, though some place it at the Antonia fortress beside the temple. Cyrene was a city in North Africa with a large Jewish community. Mark names Simon's sons Alexander and Rufus as though his readers knew them, and some connect Rufus with the Rufus greeted in Romans 16:13, though the name was common. Golgotha is Aramaic for skull, probably describing the shape of the site or its use for executions; since the fourth century the Church of the Holy Sepulchre has marked the traditional location.

The wine mixed with myrrh was a drink that dulled pain, which Jesus refused. Soldiers customarily took the clothing of the executed. Mark counts hours from sunrise: the third hour is about 9 a.m., the sixth noon, the ninth 3 p.m. The temple curtain was a great woven hanging, either the one that separated the Holy of Holies from the rest of the sanctuary or the outer one at the entrance; the first is the one the high priest passed through once a year on the Day of Atonement. Rock-cut tombs with a rolling or blocking stone were used by families who could afford them.
literary: Mark tells the crucifixion with restraint. He does not describe the physical suffering at length but lets irony carry the meaning. Every mockery speaks the truth: Jesus is the King of the Jews, he saved others and so cannot save himself, and he will rebuild the temple in three days in a way his mockers do not imagine. The account is laced with Psalm 22, the lament of a righteous sufferer: the dividing of garments (Psalm 22:18), the head-shaking mockers (22:7), and the cry of forsakenness (22:1), which Mark gives first in Aramaic and then translates. Three hours of darkness recall the plague of darkness in Egypt and Amos 8:9, where God makes the sun go down at noon. The torn curtain and the centurion's confession come together at the moment of death: God's presence is opened and a Gentile sees who Jesus is. Verse 28 is absent from the earliest manuscripts; it quotes Isaiah 53:12, as Luke 22:37 does, and was likely added by copyists.

outline.t: Darkness, the cry, the death, the torn curtain, the confession
The women watching from a distance

doctrines.note: The innocent Jesus dies while the guilty Barabbas goes free, a picture of substitution that the church has always seen at the heart of the cross. His cry of forsakenness shows that he entered the depth of separation that sin brings, and the torn curtain declares that the way into God's presence is now open. Christians confess that he died for sinners, bearing their judgment.

Mark makes Jesus' kingship the charge, the mockery, and the truth. He is crowned with thorns, saluted in scorn, and lifted up under the title King of the Jews. The kingdom of God is revealed not by his escape from the cross but by his faithfulness on it.

Jesus prays the opening of Psalm 22 in his agony. The righteous sufferer of Israel's laments finds his fullest expression in him. Believers who suffer and feel abandoned can pray the same words, knowing that Christ has prayed them first and that the psalm ends in vindication.

words.note: Stauroo, to crucify, from stauros, a stake or cross. The verb appears seven times in the chapter, from the crowd's shout to the soldiers' act. To the Roman world it named the most shameful death; the New Testament makes it the center of the gospel (1 Corinthians 1:23, 2:2).

Egkataleipo, to forsake, abandon, leave behind utterly. It is the word of Psalm 22:1 in the Greek Old Testament. Jesus' cry expresses real abandonment, felt and spoken. The church has read it as the Son bearing the weight of sin's judgment, while never teaching that the Trinity was divided in its being.

Katapetasma, curtain or veil. In the Greek Old Testament it names the curtain before the Most Holy Place (Exodus 26:31-33). Its tearing from top to bottom, from God's side, signals both judgment on the temple and access to God. Hebrews 10:19-20 develops the image: believers enter the holy places through the curtain, that is, through Christ's flesh.

Huios, son. The centurion calls Jesus Son of God, the title of Mark 1:1 and of the Father's voice at the baptism and transfiguration. In a Roman soldier's mouth the phrase might have meant a divine man or a hero; in Mark's story it is the true confession, spoken at last by a human being.

christ: Here Mark shows most clearly who Jesus is and what he has done. He is the Son of God, confessed at the cross. He is the King of the Jews, enthroned in suffering. He is the Son of Man who came not to be served but to give his life as a ransom for many (10:45), and here he gives it. The church confesses on the witness of this chapter that Jesus truly died: Pilate confirms it with the centurion, Joseph wraps the body, and the women see the tomb. That is part of the first-order confession of the creeds, that he was crucified under Pontius Pilate, died, and was buried. It is also the ground of the next chapter. Because the death was real and witnessed, the empty tomb is news.

hard.q: When Jesus cried, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” was he truly abandoned by God?
hard.a: The cry is one of the most searching moments in the Gospels, and the church has read it in several complementary ways. First, it is a quotation of Psalm 22:1, and Jewish readers often cited a psalm's first line to call to mind the whole. Psalm 22 moves from lament to trust and ends with God's rule proclaimed to the nations, so some interpreters hear in the cry not despair but faith spoken from the depths. Second, many hold that Jesus truly experienced separation from the Father's favor as he bore the judgment due to sin, citing Paul's statement that God made him who knew no sin to be sin for us (2 Corinthians 5:21) and that Christ became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). Third, theologians across traditions insist that whatever Jesus experienced, the Trinity was not broken apart: the Son did not cease to be the Son, and he still calls on my God. These readings are not rivals. The cry is real anguish, voiced in Scripture's own words, by the one who entered the full darkness of human abandonment so that those who trust him would never be forsaken.

questions: Barabbas, guilty, went free while Jesus, innocent, was crucified. How does it change your view of the cross to see yourself in Barabbas's place?
The women watched from a distance when the disciples had fled. What does faithfulness look like when you cannot change what is happening but can still stay?
The centurion saw how Jesus died and confessed him as the Son of God. What about the way Jesus died reveals who he is to you?
